citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The facility failed to maintain direct and frequent communication with the attending veterinarian regarding an adult female
goat's condition. The attending veterinarian evaluated the goat and prescribed medications for a foot abscess on
10/7/2026. He instructed the facility to give the medication daily for 7 days (so that the last day of treatment should have
been 10/14/2026). At the time of inspection, inspectors observed the goat bearing little weight on her right front leg, and
the licensee and representative said that as of yesterday (10/18/2026), they were still giving it the medication. Facility
representatives stated that they had not communicated with the AV after the course of treatment to notify him that the
animal is still lame or that they continued to give the medication after the prescription ended.
Direct and frequent communication of animal health problems, especially when an animal's condition does not improve
following treatment, is necessary to ensure adequate veterinary care and prevent unnecessary pain and distress.
The licensee must ensure that a mechanism of direct and frequent communication is in place so that timely and accurate
information on problems of animal health, behavior and well-being is conveyed to the attending veterinarian.

During review of facility disposition records, it was noted that on 10/16/26, an adult female kangaroo died while attempting
to catch it for transport to winter housing. A facility representative conveyed that an employee walked the animal into the
shelter for outdoor housing, shut the door, and then tried to grab her by the tail in the small space, approximately 8 ft by 8
ft. The representative described to APHIS officials that he then heard the kangaroo hit the wall very hard when she
jumped to get away, struck her head/neck on the wall, and died a short while later.
Failure to handle the kangaroo as carefully as possible led to physical harm and death of this animal. Handling of all
animals shall be done as expeditiously and carefully as possible in a manner that does not cause trauma, overheating,
excessive cooling, behavioral stress, physical harm, or unnecessary comfort.

Inspectors observed sharp points in two enclosures:
-An approximately 1 foot by 8 inch area of the bottom of the metal wall of a shed housing a billy goat (next to the zebra) is
folded up, creating sharp points.
-An area inside the cavy enclosure (southwest side of enclosure) contains chain-link fence-points by the ground where the
animals dig. The points are directed into the enclosure and can contact the animals as they dig.
Areas with rough and sharp edges can injure animals. Enclosures must be maintained in good repair to protect animals
from injury.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the licensee and facility representative.
You may appeal all or part of any inspection report by submitting a written statement contesting the findings—along with
any supporting documentation—to the Deputy Administrator. Appeals of routine, focused, or attempted inspections must
be received within 21 days of report issuance as shown by the signature line of this report.
Appeals may be sent by email to AnimalCare@usda.gov.
Appeals sent by mail should be addressed to:

Mailstop #3W11
